clue.text: The sort of woman who wants everything sewn up

definitions.text: The sort of woman who wants everything sewn up

parts.words: The sort of woman who wants everything sewn up
parts.note: 'sewn up' reads as slang for settled or sorted, but taken literally it is the needlework a dressmaker finishes

explanation.surface: A controlling woman who likes every deal settled and nothing left to chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewn up' sounds like a deal settled in advance; read literally, it is the stitching done by someone who sews for a living.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman whose trade is sewing naturally wants every garment stitched, a literal reading of the idiom.

clue.text: Seat used by person of authority

indicators.note: used by means the answer is held within the following words, which carry it among their letters

explanation.surface: A chair reserved for the boss or some other official.
explanation.walkthrough: As printed, 'person of authority' does not contain the answer; the setter's 'persons of authority' does, across the end of 'persons', 'of' and the start of 'authority'.
explanation.definitionFit: A couch is an upholstered seat for two or more people.

clue.text: Forgetful of a maiden since breaking up

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

indicators.note: breaking up means the letters of the word since fall apart and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone has lost their memory of a young woman ever since they split up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking up' sounds like a relationship ending, but here it tells you to scramble a word. M for maiden comes from cricket scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone suffering amnesia, loss of memory, is forgetful.

clue.text: May no travails disrupt those helping the homeless at Christmas!

definitions.text: those helping the homeless at Christmas

indicators.note: disrupt asks the solver to break up the order of the letters in may no travails and rebuild them

explanation.surface: A festive wish that no hardships interfere with charity workers caring for rough sleepers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disrupt' signals an anagram of MAY NO TRAVAILS; the surface's hope that nothing gets in their way is itself a nod to the charity.
explanation.definitionFit: The Christian charity is famous for its shelters and Christmas appeals for people sleeping rough.

clue.text: Sold, like the party donkey (not for the first time!)

definitions.text: like the party donkey (not for the first time!)

explanation.surface: A shop sold goods, rather like the donkey in a children's party game.
explanation.walkthrough: In the party game 'pin the tail on the donkey' the donkey gets its tail again and again, so it is tailed a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods passed to shoppers in a store are retailed, i.e. sold; and a donkey given its tail again has been tailed anew.

clue.text: Turn away from football team after final change of direction

indicators.note: final change of says the last letter of the team name is swapped for another letter

parts.note: Spurs is the nickname of Tottenham Hotspur, a London football club
N is north, a compass direction

explanation.surface: A footballer turns away from his old team after a late U-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: SPURS is Tottenham Hotspur, a London football club. 'final change of' swaps its last letter, S, for N (north, the 'direction').
explanation.definitionFit: To reject someone or something scornfully is to turn away from it.

clue.text: Hands back exchanged gift

indicators.note: back says the word for hands is read from right to left

parts.note: paws is a jokey word for hands

explanation.surface: Someone hands back an unwanted present that had been exchanged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands back' looks like returning something; it is PAWS (hands) read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A thing traded for another in a straight exchange is a trade item, the noun sense of the word.

clue.text: English gentleman in court, almost completely poker-faced

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them

indicators.note: almost completely means the last letter of the word for poker-faced is left off

parts.note: stern describes a grim, expressionless face

explanation.surface: A gentleman stands in a law court with an almost wholly expressionless face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court' is a verb, not a law court. Bertie Wooster is P G Wodehouse's comic English gentleman, master of Jeeves.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertie of the Wodehouse novels is the archetypal amiable upper-class English toff.

clue.text: Quiet nerds, fine when mixing — writers, rather than talkers?

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

indicators.note: mixing tells the solver to stir together the letters of quiet, nerds and fine

explanation.surface: Shy geeks get along fine when they socialise, but prefer writing to chatting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixing' sounds like socialising, but it is the anagram signal. 'writers, rather than talkers?' plays on friends who only write to each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Correspondents who exchange letters keep in touch by writing rather than by talking.

clue.text: Big match excellent, with a fifty for Essex's opener

indicators.note: for means one thing is put in place of another, here the opening letter of Essex

parts.note: fine means excellent

indicators.note: opener means the first letter of the word Essex's

parts.note: A plus L, the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Essex's opening batsman scores a fine fifty in an important cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface points to a batsman; really the E of 'Essex's opener' in FINE is replaced by A and L (Roman fifty).
explanation.definitionFit: The deciding game of a competition is its biggest match.

clue.text: Landing somewhere in Holland, as Spooner would have it?

indicators.note: as Spooner would have it means the opening sounds of the two words are swapped

parts.note: any town in the Netherlands is a Dutch town
any town in the Netherlands is a Dutch town

explanation.surface: An aircraft lands somewhere in the Netherlands.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the first sounds of DUTCH TOWN and it says TUTCH DOWN, spelt as the aviation word.
explanation.definitionFit: The moment an aircraft's wheels meet the runway is its arrival on the ground.

clue.text: A rev (no heathen) organised divine bliss down here

indicators.note: organised tells the solver to put the letters of a rev no heathen into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A vicar, with no pagans present, arranged a heavenly celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organised' signals an anagram of A REV NO HEATHEN; the brackets only hide the fodder within a church scene.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes perfect happiness, paradise experienced in this world.

clue.text: Rattiest man so upset railway employee

indicators.note: upset means the letters of rattiest man so are overturned and rearranged

explanation.surface: The grumpiest man becomes even more annoyed, perhaps on the railway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reads as angry but signals an anagram of RATTIEST MAN SO.
explanation.definitionFit: The official in charge of a railway stop works for the railway.

clue.text: Consume a pork-pie thing after surprising event?

definitions.text: Consume a pork-pie thing after surprising event?

parts.words: Consume a pork-pie thing after surprising event?
parts.note: a pork-pie is a flat-crowned headgear; swallowing your own after being proved wrong is the promise in a well-known idiom

explanation.surface: Someone eats a pork pie after a shock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pork-pie' suggests food, but it is a style of flat-crowned hat; people say they will consume their headgear if something unlikely happens.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom expresses total disbelief that something will occur, offering to swallow headwear if it does.

clue.text: Put down a little son on manger — the lord finally seen

parts.note: S is the short form of son
a crib is a manger, the feeding trough of the Nativity

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of each of the words the and lord

explanation.surface: A nativity scene: a baby son is laid in a manger and the Lord is at last revealed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nativity picture hides the parts: A, S (son), CRIB (manger) and E and D, the last letters of 'the lord'.
explanation.definitionFit: To attribute something to a cause is to put it down to that cause.

clue.text: Not much of a turn? It gets an award at Edinburgh, maybe

explanation.surface: A modest performance on stage still wins a prize at the Edinburgh Festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' and 'award at Edinburgh' suggest a festival act; really it is a small angle and a university qualification.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny angle of rotation is one 360th of a circle; and a university, such as Edinburgh, confers an academic qualification.

clue.text: Feeling great excitement? No, by implication!

parts.note: the clue word no is the result of a pair of letters flipped round, so it is the wordplay's output

explanation.surface: Asked if they feel thrilled, someone says no, but implies the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: ON when TURNED gives NO, so 'No' is what the answer would make if read as instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: Being aroused or excited by something is the phrasal verb's slang sense.

clue.text: Flowering plant that has yellow wood

parts.note: or is gold or yellow in heraldry
pine is a type of timber

explanation.surface: A plant with yellow wood.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic word for gold or yellow; ORPINE is a stonecrop with pink flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: The stonecrop called livelong is a succulent herb that bears purple-pink blooms.

clue.text: Plant that's a favourite, one picked by woman

parts.note: a pet is a favourite, as in teacher's pet

indicators.note: picked by means the word for one is taken into the woman's name

parts.note: Una is a woman's name
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A woman picks the flower that is her favourite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked by' makes the woman hold the one, as if she had chosen it. The Roman numeral gives the one.
explanation.definitionFit: This garden flower with trumpet-shaped blooms is a bedding plant.

clue.text: Odd, the newspaper boss we work for, it's said (in a gossipy way)

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange

parts.words: the newspaper boss we work for
parts.note: our editor, ED being the usual short form of editor

explanation.surface: Gossip in the newsroom says their editor is rather peculiar.
explanation.walkthrough: RUM is old-fashioned British slang for strange; 'the newspaper boss we work for' is OUR ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Reported as hearsay is how the gossip mill passes on a story.

clue.text: Sailors — they matter to broadcasters

explanation.surface: Seamen are important to the people who make television.
explanation.walkthrough: Ordinary sailors below officer rank are ratings in the Royal Navy; viewing figures are too.
explanation.definitionFit: Naval seamen without commissions are known by this term; and audience figures decide a show's success for TV channels.

clue.text: Ten nattier men out to offer fun

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of ten nattier men are thrown out of order and rearranged

explanation.surface: Ten smartly dressed men head out on the town to amuse people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' looks like going out for the evening; it signals an anagram of TEN NATTIER MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Amusement or enjoyment is what a show or party provides.

clue.text: Affair in which a maiden joining open university gets tutor, finally

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
OU is the Open University, the UK's distance-learning university

indicators.note: finally means the last letter of the word tutor

explanation.surface: A young woman studying with the Open University ends up in a romance with her tutor.
explanation.walkthrough: The Open University is Britain's distance-learning university, abbreviated OU. M, the maiden, comes from cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A love affair, especially a secret one, borrows the French word for love.

clue.text: Little woman eager (not half) to get something in cracker

parts.note: Jo is a heroine of Little Women

indicators.note: not half means only the first half of the word for eager is kept

parts.note: keen means eager

explanation.surface: A small girl is half-hearted about getting something from a Christmas cracker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little woman' is Jo March of the novel Little Women. A Christmas cracker is a paper tube pulled at British Christmas dinners, holding a paper hat and a corny riddle.
explanation.definitionFit: Christmas crackers traditionally contain a groan-worthy pun or riddle printed on a slip.

clue.text: Mass-producer establishing poultry unit by railway crossing

parts.note: a hen is a single bird of the poultry flock
a ford is a shallow river crossing

explanation.surface: Someone setting up a chicken farm next to a level crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: The American carmaker pioneered assembly-line mass production with the Model T.
explanation.definitionFit: The motor magnate introduced the moving assembly line, making cars in vast numbers.

clue.text: Moody attending party? You want some music

parts.note: Ron Moody was the British actor who played Fagin in the film Oliver!
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Someone sulky going to a party wants some music played.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moody' looks like a mood but is the actor Ron Moody, famous as Fagin in Oliver!, giving RON.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece with a recurring main theme is a musical form often used in sonata finales.

clue.text: Audibly scoff at meals

indicators.note: audibly means the word for scoff at is spoken, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: to tease is to mock or scoff at

explanation.surface: Someone noisily jeers at the food served.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scoff' tempts as eating greedily, which suits 'meals'; here it means mock, TEASE, said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Afternoon or evening light repasts are called by the name of the drink served.

clue.text: Chief earns pots as one granted a special concession

indicators.note: pots, as in taking random shots, signals that the letters of chief earns are scattered and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A boss makes money by winning at snooker as a special favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pots' looks like snooker winnings; it signals an anagram of CHIEF EARNS.
explanation.definitionFit: A business licensed to trade under another company's brand holds an exclusive commercial right.
